title: Secure Agentic Access to AWS with Enterprise-Managed Authorization
content:
AWS Security Blog
Secure agentic access to AWS with Enterprise-Managed Authorization
AWS Sign-In is introducing support for Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) using the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), enabling organizations to securely authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server through their existing enterprise identity providers (IdPs), such as Okta. With this capability, organizations can centrally manage which applications can access Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources on behalf of their employees, without requiring users to manage additional long-term credentials or complete separate consent flows.
In our previous blog post, Introducing OAuth Support for AWS MCP Server, we introduced OAuth-based authorization, enabling AI agents to securely access AWS MCP Server through interactive sign-in or programmatic authentication using AWS credentials. EMA builds on these capabilities by enabling organizations to authorize AI agents through their existing enterprise IdPs. Because authentication to an AI application doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources, EMA provides a way to authorize access across these separate trust domains while maintaining existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions.
In this post, we explain how EMA and ID-JAG work with AWS Sign-In, discuss security best practices, and walk you through configuring Okta to authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server.
How Enterprise-Managed Authorization works with AWS Sign-In
Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) is an extension of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enables organizations to centrally manage how AI applications access protected resources on behalf of employees. EMA uses the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), an OAuth-based authorization grant that enables enterprise IdPs to authorize access across different trust domains. Rather than requiring employees to individually authorize each MCP server, administrators can define policies in their existing IdP to control which AI applications can access specific resources.
When an employee signs in to an AI application such as Claude using their enterprise IdP, the authentication establishes their identity within Claude but doesn’t automatically grant access to AWS resources. When the AI application requests access to an MCP server, the enterprise IdP evaluates its configured access policies and issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion for the intended resource. The AI application then exchanges this assertion with the authorization server configured for the MCP server to obtain an OAuth access token, without requiring the employee to complete an additional interactive authorization flow.
For AWS MCP Server, AWS Sign-In serves as the configured OAuth authorization server. The AI application presents the ID-JAG assertion to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. As part of the authorization process, AWS validates the assertion against the trusted IdP and uses AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to evaluate the IAM role’s trust policy and establish the authorized role session. AWS Sign-In then issues an OAuth access token associated with the IAM role. IAM policies attached to the role determine which AWS operations the agent can perform, allowing organizations to manage agent authorization through their enterprise IdP while enforcing existing AWS permissions.
Figure 1 illustrates how an AI application, such as Claude, uses EMA with Okta and AWS Sign-In to obtain an OAuth access token and securely access AWS MCP Server using IAM role-based permissions.
The authorization flow consists of the following steps, as illustrated in Figure 1:
- Employee authentication: The employee signs in to the AI application, such as Claude, using their enterprise IdP, such as Okta, through single sign-on (SSO).
- ID-JAG request: When the AI application needs to access AWS MCP Server, it requests an ID-JAG from Okta for the intended resource.
- Enterprise authorization: Okta evaluates the configured access policies to determine whether the employee and AI application are authorized to access AWS MCP Server. If authorized, Okta issues a short-lived, signed ID-JAG assertion.
- Token exchange with AWS Sign-In: The AI application sends the ID-JAG to the AWS Sign-In OAuth token endpoint. AWS Sign-In validates the assertion, including its issuer, signature, audience/tenant, expiration, and intended resource, and verifies the associated IAM role authorization before issuing an OAuth access token.
- Access AWS MCP Server: The AI application presents the AWS-issued OAuth access token to AWS MCP Server. The server validates the token, and access to AWS resources is governed by the permissions associated with the IAM role.
Configure Enterprise-Managed Authorization using Okta and AWS Sign-In
In this section, we walk you through configuring Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) to enable an AI application, such as Claude, to securely access AWS MCP Server using an enterprise identity managed in Okta.
The configuration establishes trust between Okta and AWS, defines IAM permissions for accessing AWS resources, and configures enterprise authorization policies that govern AI application access. This walkthrough uses AWS MCP Server in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region (us-west-2).
Prerequisites
Before you begin, make sure you have the following:
- An AWS account with permissions to configure IAM IdPs, roles, and policies.
- An Okta organization with administrative permissions to manage applications and configure Cross-App Access policies.
- An AI application, such as Claude, that supports EMA and ID-JAG.
- Access to AWS MCP Server with support for OAuth-based Enterprise-Managed Authorization.
- The AWS Region where you will configure the integration.
Step 0: Configure the AI application in Okta
Configure an application in Okta so that employees can sign in to the AI application through enterprise single sign-on (SSO). For this walkthrough, we use Claude as the AI application. If your organization already uses Claude with Okta SSO, you can use the existing application. This application is the requesting application when you configure Cross-App Access in Step 3.
- Create the Claude SSO application: In the Okta Admin Console, go to Applications, choose Create App Integration, and create an OIDC web application, for example Claude SSO, as shown in Figure 2. 
         
  - If your agent was imported through an Okta AI Agent Provider, create the OIDC application by going to Directory, AI Agents, then navigating to User access from the selected agent.
- Choose the grant types: Select Authorization Code and Refresh Token. Claude uses the refresh token to request new ID-JAG assertions without asking employees to sign in again.
- Add the redirect URI: Set Sign-in redirect URIs to Claude’s SSO callback URL.
- Assign employees: Under Assignments, select which employees or groups can access the application.
- Confirm SSO works: Check that employees can sign in to Claude through Okta before you continue.
Step 1: Configure Okta as an OIDC IdP in IAM
Create an OpenID Connect (OIDC) IdP so that AWS trusts the ID-JAG assertions that Okta issues, as shown in Figure 3.
- Add the IdP: In the AWS Management Console for IAM, go to Identity providers, choose Add provider, and select OpenID Connect.
- Enter the provider URL: For Provider URL, enter your Okta org URL, for example https://integrator-1234567.okta.com. Okta issues ID-JAG assertions from the org authorization server, not from a custom authorization server.
- Enter the audience: For Audience, enter the AWS Sign-In authorization server for your Region, for example https://us-west-2.oauth.signin.aws, and choose Add provider.
Step 2: Create an IAM role and configure permissions
Create an IAM role that defines the AWS permissions granted to the AI application, as shown in Figure 4.
- Create the role: In the IAM console, go to Roles, choose Create role, and select We

report.summary: AWS Sign-In now supports Enterprise-Managed Authorization via ID-JAG, letting organizations centrally authorize AI agents to access AWS MCP Server through identity providers like Okta.
report.background: AI agents increasingly connect to enterprise systems through MCP, but authentication and authorization are separate trust domains: signing into an AI app does not grant cloud access. Previously, AWS MCP Server OAuth support let agents access AWS via interactive sign-in or programmatic AWS credentials. Enterprises wanted central control, avoiding long-lived credentials and per-user consent flows. EMA extends MCP; ID-JAG is an OAuth grant for enterprise IdPs to issue short-lived assertions across domains. AWS Sign-In acts as the OAuth authorization server for AWS MCP Server. The announcement builds on AWS's earlier OAuth work and reflects a broader push to make agent identity, delegation, and auditability first-class enterprise concerns.
key_points: EMA is an MCP extension that lets administrators define IdP policies controlling which AI applications can access specific resources on employees' behalf. Instead of each user consenting to each MCP server, Okta or another IdP evaluates policy and issues a short-lived signed ID-JAG assertion. AWS Sign-In validates it and issues an OAuth token tied to an IAM role.

The authorization flow separates identity from cloud permission. An employee SSOs into an AI app like Claude; the app requests an ID-JAG from Okta for AWS MCP Server; Okta checks Cross-App Access policy; AWS Sign-In validates issuer, signature, audience, expiry, and resource, then uses STS to establish an IAM role session. IAM policies still govern what the agent can do.

Setup requires trust configuration on both sides: an Okta OIDC app for the AI application with authorization code and refresh token grants, an AWS IAM OIDC identity provider pointing to the Okta org URL and AWS Sign-In audience, an IAM role with least-privilege policies, and Okta Cross-App Access policies authorizing the app-to-resource exchange.

Security benefits include no long-lived AWS credentials for agents, no separate per-user consent flow, short-lived assertions and tokens, centralized revocation and policy control through the IdP, and continued enforcement of existing IAM permissions. The approach is aimed at production agent deployments where auditability and least privilege matter.
report.impact: For the AI industry, EMA signals that agent authorization is converging on OAuth-based delegation and enterprise IdP control rather than bespoke API keys. It could make MCP servers easier to adopt in regulated enterprises because security teams can reuse Okta policies, SSO, and IAM. Developers get a standard flow—ID-JAG exchange with AWS Sign-In—but must handle token refresh, assertion validation, and least-privilege roles. Regular users benefit from fewer consent prompts and no extra credentials, though access depends on admin policy. The main constraint is ecosystem support: IdPs, AI apps, and MCP servers must implement EMA/ID-JAG. AWS's move may pressure other cloud and SaaS providers to support similar cross-domain agent authorization.
report.tools: Follow AWS MCP Server OAuth/EMA docs, AWS IAM OIDC identity providers and STS, Okta Cross-App Access and AI Agents, and the Model Context Protocol spec. For hands-on testing, use Claude as an EMA-capable AI app, an Okta developer org, and an AWS test account with scoped IAM roles. Watch ID-JAG implementations and MCP authorization extensions; open-source MCP clients/servers that add EMA support will be useful for local experiments.
